title: The Old Folks
lines: I will tell you a tale about old folks, children, so listen!
Once a soldier, home from the army, was walking and walking on his way home,
and as he went through a village, he saw
a white-haired old man sitting out by the gate,
crying so bitterly that the whole village rang with it.
The soldier asked him:
"Why ever are you crying, grandad?"
"Oh, how could I not cry, my dear son, when my father has given me a beating."
"You don't say!
Why, you must be a hundred years old yourself. Surely your father is not alive?"
"Well, if you don't believe me, son, go into the yard.
Look, my father is chopping wood right now!"
The soldier went in, and there truly was an even older man,
chopping wood better than any young lad could have.
The soldier greeted him:
"Good day to you, grandad!
However could you have the heart to beat your son?"
"Why should I not have beaten him, when he did not obey his grandfather!"
"Well, well, what are you saying?!
So your father is still alive too?"
"Of course he is!
Just go into the house, he is sitting by the stove, smoking his pipe.
Go and see, if you don't believe me!"
The soldier went in.
And there truly was the old man, sitting by the stove.
He was puffing big clouds of smoke from his pipe and grumbling about his grandson,
that if the boy disobeyed him just once more, he would really give it to him.
The soldier greeted the old man and asked:
"Tell me, dear old grandfather, how old might you be?"
"Oh, my dear son, that I do not know.
But go to the priest who baptised me.
He will look it up in the parish book."
"Come now, grandad, don't joke. Surely the priest who baptised you is not still alive?"
"He is, by God, so help me Christ, he is alive, son.
If you don't believe me, go and see!
You will surely find him at home, he is always reading the Bible."
The soldier went to the priest.
And there he truly was, sitting at the table.
In front of him lay the old Bible.
On his nose was a big pair of spectacles, and he was mumbling and reading from it.
"A good and happy day to you, reverend father!"
"Welcome, my dear son!
What brings you here?
Are you perhaps getting married?"
"Not now, reverend father,
but I would like to know how old such-and-such an old man might be."
"Well, my dear son, I cannot know that without the book,
but I will look it up in the parish book at once."
The priest stood up.
He went to his bookcase to take out the parish book.
But oh!
The bookcase was locked.
"Well, my dear son," said the priest, "I am very sorry,
but I cannot take out the parish book, because the key is not at home.
My mother took it with her to the vineyard!"
If the priest's mother had not taken the key, my tale would have gone on longer too.
Here is the end, run off with it!
